qs.q: During auscultation of a patient with suspected acute pericarditis, a high-pitched scratchy or squeaky sound is best heard with the diaphragm at the left sternal border. What does this friction rub correspond to?
o: Atrial systole, ventricular systole, and early diastole
Isovolumetric contraction, rapid ejection, and atrial kick
First heart sound, second heart sound, and a third heart sound
Ventricular filling, passive diastole, and atrial repolarization
qs.e: A pericardial friction rub has three components which correspond to atrial systole, ventricular systole, and early diastole. It is a key sign present in a majority of acute pericarditis cases.

qs.q: A patient with Hodgkin lymphoma has disease on both sides of the diaphragm involving multiple lymph node groups and the spleen, with no systemic symptoms. What is his Ann Arbor stage and what does the absence of systemic symptoms signify?
o: A. Stage III-A — disease on both sides of diaphragm including spleen, no systemic symptoms
B. Stage II-A — disease on same side of diaphragm, no systemic symptoms
C. Stage IV-B — disseminated disease with no systemic symptoms
D. Stage III-B — disease on both sides of diaphragm with systemic symptoms
qs.e: Stage III involves lymph node regions on both sides of the diaphragm; the S suffix denotes splenic involvement giving Stage IIIS. The suffix A indicates absence of systemic symptoms (fever, night sweats, unexplained >10% weight loss). Stage B would indicate presence of these symptoms. Stage IV requires disseminated extralymphatic organ involvement which is not described here.

qs.q: A neonate presents with regurgitation during the first feeding, aspiration, and abdominal distention from gas below the diaphragm. What is the most likely oesophageal abnormality and its most common variant?
o: Oesophageal atresia alone with no distal fistula
Oesophageal atresia with distal tracheoesophageal fistula
qs.e: The most common variant is oesophageal atresia with a distal tracheoesophageal fistula. Gas below the diaphragm indicates a distal fistula allowing air into the GI tract.

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The diaphragm is a dome‑shaped muscle that separates the thoracic and abdominal cavities, essential for breathing and protecting abdominal organs. Its function, innervation, and clinical significance are key for clinicians.

sections.p: The diaphragm is the primary inspiratory muscle, forming a partition between the thorax and abdomen. It contracts to increase thoracic volume and decrease pressure, drawing air into the lungs.
It spans the lower thoracic cavity, attaching to the lower ribs, sternum, and lumbar vertebrae. The central tendon is a fibroelastic core.
Anteriorly it lies over the liver and stomach; posteriorly it is adjacent to the kidneys and spleen. The phrenic nerve and major vessels cross its surface.
b: Azygos vein runs along right side

sections.p: Arterial supply comes from the phrenic, intercostal, and musculophrenic arteries.
The phrenic nerve provides motor and sensory fibers; sympathetic fibers from the thoracic sympathetic chain also contribute.
During inspiration, contraction flattens the dome, increasing thoracic volume and decreasing intrathoracic pressure. It also assists in forced expiration and protects abdominal organs.
Diaphragmatic hernias, paralysis, and trauma can impair ventilation and abdominal organ function. In low‑resource settings, delayed diagnosis may lead to respiratory failure.
b: Traumatic rupture: often missed on X‑ray

t.b: Shows flattened diaphragm or free air under diaphragm; indicates rupture or hernia
Rapid bedside detection of diaphragmatic motion; useful when X‑ray unavailable
Gold standard for occult diaphragmatic injury; confirms herniation and guides surgery

sections.p: Ask about sudden dyspnea after trauma, abdominal pain, or bowel sounds in the chest. A normal chest X‑ray does not rule out a diaphragmatic tear; consider ultrasound or CT.
b: Trauma + chest pain + abdominal bruit = suspect tear

faq.a: Common causes include phrenic nerve injury from neck trauma, cervical spinal cord lesions, or inflammatory neuropathies.

faq.q: How is a diaphragmatic hernia diagnosed in a low‑resource setting?
faq.a: Look for bowel sounds in the chest and use bedside ultrasound to detect abnormal diaphragmatic motion.

faq.q: Why does the diaphragm flatten in tension pneumothorax?
faq.a: Increased intrathoracic pressure pushes the diaphragm downward, flattening it and shifting the mediastinum.
